cvOptimizer.title: CV Optimizer Pro
cvOptimizer.sub: An agent system that interviews you and builds a CV you can defend in a real interview.
shots: CV Optimizer coach interview and its feedback card. Fictional data.
Credibility auditor report with two flags. Fictional data.
Optimized CV already generated. Fictional data.
Job listing analysis with the matching percentage. Fictional data.
problem: When I wrote my CV I didn't know what to tell. There were things I did every day and didn't value. Leading 2 people was one of them.
The tools I tried did the opposite. They inflated everything, and that falls apart at the first interview question.
cvOptimizer.pipelineAria: The interview with the AI coach builds the profile, the auditor reviews what has no backing, it is matched against the job posting and an ATS CV comes out.
steps: Interview
An AI coach asks about your experience. Every answer leads to a new question and it never repeats itself. If you already have a CV, you upload the PDF or DOCX and it pre-fills the profile.
Audit
An agent reviews what you said and flags what you can't back up or what you're underselling.
Match and CV
You paste a job posting, see the fit and generate the tailored CV with its keyword report.
decisions: The auditor has the last word. An achievement with no backing doesn't make it into the CV.
One column, Arial and no graphics, so ATS systems read all of it.
Each interview phase has a turn limit and shows progress, so it never drags on.
cvOptimizer.result: I use it with my own profile. The CV I apply with today came out of it, and the interview is what made me see that leading 2 devs was an achievement.

jobHunter.title: Job Hunter Platform
jobHunter.sub: A platform that checks job boards for me, ranks listings against my profile and builds the CV for each one.
shots: Job Hunter dashboard with the listings ranking. Fictional data.
Expanded listing with requirements and matching skills. Fictional data.
Application preview with the CV in several formats. Fictional data.
AI token usage panel and monthly cost. Fictional data.
problem: Job hunting meant checking the same boards every day and reading listings that didn't fit me.
I wanted a system to do that first pass and leave me only the ones worth reading.
jobHunter.pipelineAria: Three job boards are checked every two hours with Celery, listings are stored in PostgreSQL, OpenAI scores the fit and the result goes to a dashboard.
steps: Collection
Three scrapers check RemoteOK, WeWorkRemotely and GetOnBoard every 2 hours with Celery Beat and store listings in a common format.
Ranking
OpenAI compares each listing with my profile and assigns a fit score.
Applying
From the dashboard I pick a listing and generate a tailored CV, with a version built for ATS.
decisions: It runs on Celery with Redis, so no slow board holds up the dashboard.
Each scraper maps its board to the same PostgreSQL model. Adding a board means writing one new class.
Listings, profile, CV, applications and notifications each have their own FastAPI router.
jobHunter.result: It runs fully on local Docker Compose: API, worker, database and dashboard.

gpsAnalyzer.title: GPS Analyzer
gpsAnalyzer.sub: A GPS transmission health analyzer. It showed which providers and vehicles were failing, with the evidence one click away.
shots: Clients view with tiles for clients with critical status and no data. Fictional data.
Providers view with their score and the share of the fleet in good shape. Fictional data.
Vehicle detail with the score, last transmission and open failure. Fictional data.
Send frequency and offset between the GPS and the provider. Fictional data.
problem: When a provider stopped transmitting properly, we found out from the client's complaint. By then it was late.
I wanted an operator to answer in under 1 minute which providers are failing and why, without reading raw data.
gpsAnalyzer.pipelineAria: Raw provider data enters a batch engine that stores metrics, failures F01 to F11 are detected, a 6-dimension score is computed and the result goes to a dashboard.
steps: Ingestion
An incremental engine reads each provider's raw data and stores counters and histograms that can be re-aggregated.
Detection and score
The engine classifies the day's failures and computes a 0 to 100 score per vehicle. Thresholds are applied at query time.
Dashboard
The operator starts at the client, drills into the provider and reaches the vehicle with the evidence and what to do about each failure.
decisions: Atomic metrics are stored and thresholds are applied at query time. Moving a threshold recomputes the score without rereading the source.
The landing page sorts by affected client, because that is how a complaint gets handled.
If a dimension is missing, the score is computed on the measurable points and the screen says so.
gpsAnalyzer.result: It was used for daily transmission follow-up until it was retired. I learned to design an engine where the rule moves and the data stays untouched.

pokemonTcgai.title: pokemontcgai
pokemonTcgai.sub: An agent that plays Pokémon TCG for the Kaggle Pokémon TCG AI Battle Challenge, with an interface so I can play against it myself.
shots: Start of a game against the model with the play log. Fictional data.
Turn 10 with the model's bench full and the attack option. Fictional data.
Turn 8 with the log of what the model would have played. Fictional data.
Finished game with the summary of the model's decisions. Fictional data.
problem: A card-game agent can't be tested with metrics alone. I had to sit down and play against it to see where it went wrong.
I wanted a rules engine faithful to the game and a way to measure the model against my own decisions.
pokemonTcgai.pipelineAria: A rules engine simulates the game, the model searches and evaluates plays, a lab tests decks, the ladder validates and an interface lets me play against the model.
steps: Engine
A rules engine with the card to effect map simulates each turn just like the game.
Search
The model evaluates the possible plays and picks one. A lab compares decks before one is submitted.
Playing against it
A web interface lets me play the model, save the session and analyze where we agree and where we don't.
decisions: Without a faithful engine, no model number is worth anything. That is why the engine has its own correctness tests.
The interface saves every session to compare my decisions with the model's.
Decks live in CSV and are tested in the lab, without touching the agent's code.
pokemonTcgai.result: The agent already plays full games and I can face it myself. Each saved session tells me which play to fix first.

projectHub.title: Project Hub
projectHub.sub: A local dashboard that gathers the progress of all my projects and tells me what comes next.
shots: Portfolio with global progress, alerts and what comes next. Fictional data.
Project detail with mandatory capabilities and their progress. Fictional data.
What's next list, with the next task and why it goes first. Fictional data.
Team view with the tickets in progress and the ones waiting for a reply. Fictional data.
problem: With several projects at once, I lost track of which one was stalled and which task came next.
I wanted a single screen that said so, without opening every repo and every ticket.
projectHub.pipelineAria: A scanner reads the repos, each project has a YAML record, Jira is queried read-only, a FastAPI API joins it all and an Angular dashboard shows it.
steps: Record
Each project is described in a YAML with its capabilities, mandatory or optional.
Scan
A scanner reads the repos and pulls the Jira tickets, always read-only.
What's next
The dashboard orders the tasks, mandatory first, and explains why one goes before another.
decisions: Jira and the repos are only read. The dashboard never changes anything outside.
Each task says why it goes first, so the order can be argued with.
It runs on 127.0.0.1 and never leaves my machine.
projectHub.result: I open it every morning to decide what to work on. It warns me about what's stalled before I notice.
